title: K-means, Gaussian mixtures, and soft assignments

items.title: K-means objective
items.statement:
Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ be observed vectors, and let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$ be centers. A labeling is a vector $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$, and its $k$th cluster is $C_k(z):=\{i:z_i=k\}$. For $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\in\mathbb R^p$, set $\|v\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^p v_j^2$. The K-means objective is

$$J(z,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K):=\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-\mu_{z_i}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k(z)}\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2.$$

An empty cluster contributes zero to the sum.
items.strategy: Definition: specify the finite labeled data, centers, coordinatewise squared Euclidean distance, within-cluster sum, and zero contribution from empty clusters.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

items.title: Finite Gaussian mixture with positive-definite component covariances
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$. Define the component function

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma):=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

The component law is $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, the $p$-dimensional normal law with mean $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. The separate local normalization result proves that $\phi_p$ is its Lebesgue density.

A finite $K$-component Gaussian mixture has an integer $K\ge1$, weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K>0$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$, means $\mu_k\in\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariance matrices $\Sigma_k\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Its density is

$$f_\theta(x):=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\phi_p(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k),$$

where $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$. For a positive integer $n$ and an ordered sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ modeled as conditionally independent observations from this mixture, define the likelihood $L(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\prod_{i=1}^n f_\theta(x_i)$ and log likelihood $\ell(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log f_\theta(x_i)$. The responsibility weight of component $k$ for observation $x_i$ is

$$\gamma_{ik}(\theta):=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}.$$
items.strategy: Definition: specify the positive-weight SPD Gaussian component formula, finite mixture, iid-sample likelihood, and normalized component responsibilities; density normalization is supplied by the local spectral-root theorem.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

items.title: Strict concavity of log determinant on positive-definite matrices
items.statement:
Let $p\ge1$ and let $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices. For $0<t<1$ and $A_0\ne A_1$,

$$\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)>(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1.$$

If $A_0=A_1$, equality holds. Thus $A\mapsto\log\det A$ is strictly concave on the positive-definite cone.
items.strategy: Differentiate log det along an SPD line by Jacobi’s formula, differentiate again using the inverse derivative, show the Hessian is a strictly negative sum of squares for every nonzero symmetric direction, then derive the strict chord inequality.

references.title: Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, §3.1.5, printed p. 74

items.title: Equal-spherical mixture assignments and objective converge to k-means
items.statement:
Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$, and fix positive weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$. Put $d_{ik}:=\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2$, $d_i^*:=\min_{1\le k\le K}d_{ik}$, and $M_i:=\{k:d_{ik}=d_i^*\}$. For every $\sigma>0$, define the normalized soft-assignment weights

$$\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}:=\frac{\pi_k\exp(-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2))}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\exp(-d_{ij}/(2\sigma^2))}$$

and the finite-data objective

$$\Psi_\sigma:=-2\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\exp(-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2))\right).$$

As $\sigma\downarrow0$, for each $i$ and $k$,

$$\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}\longrightarrow\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\pi_k}{\sum_{j\in M_i}\pi_j},&k\in M_i,\\[6pt]0,&k\notin M_i,\end{cases}$$

and

$$\Psi_\sigma\longrightarrow\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^*=\min_{z\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n}\sum_{i=1}^n d_{i,z_i}.$$

Thus a unique nearest center receives limiting weight one, while tied nearest centers divide limiting weight in proportion to their fixed mixture weights. This is a fixed-parameter finite-data limit and asserts no convergence of EM iterates.
items.strategy: Factor the minimum squared distance from each finite softmax denominator; the nearest-center weights remain as a positive finite sum, giving proportional tie limits and convergence of the scaled log-sum-exp objective.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing, Exercise 13.1
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §9.3.2 and Exercise 9.11

items.title: Lloyd's k-means algorithm with explicit tie handling
items.statement:
**Input.** Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, and supply initial centers $\mu_1^{(0)},\ldots,\mu_K^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^p$.

**Initialization.** Assign each $x_i$ to a nearest initial center, choosing the smallest center index in a tie. Denote these labels by $z_i^{(0)}$.

**Iteration.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$:

1. With the current centers fixed, assign each $x_i$ to a nearest center. If its current label $z_i^{(t)}$ is among the nearest-center indices, retain $z_i^{(t)}$; otherwise choose the smallest nearest-center index. Call the resulting labels $z_i^{(t+1)}$.
2. For each nonempty cluster $C_k^{(t+1)}:=\{i:z_i^{(t+1)}=k\}$, set
   $$\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{|C_k^{(t+1)}|}\sum_{i\in C_k^{(t+1)}}x_i.$$
   If $C_k^{(t+1)}$ is empty, set $\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\mu_k^{(t)}$.
3. If both $z^{(t+1)}=z^{(t)}$ and $\mu^{(t+1)}=\mu^{(t)}$, return these labels and centers. Otherwise continue with the updated labels and centers.

The procedure makes no global-minimization claim. Its termination under these tie rules is proved separately.
items.strategy: Procedure: initialize by nearest center with smallest-index ties, retain current labels on later ties, update nonempty centers to their means, preserve empty centers, and stop only when labels and centers both stabilize.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

items.title: Positive-definite multivariate Gaussian density is normalized
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, let $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_p$ be independent standard normal random variables, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_p)^{\mathsf T}$, and set $X=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$, where $\Sigma^{1/2}$ is the symmetric positive-definite square root. Then the law of $X$ has Lebesgue density

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

In particular, $\phi_p$ is nonnegative and $\int_{\mathbb R^p}\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=1$.
items.strategy: Diagonalize the SPD covariance, form its symmetric positive square root, identify the product standard-normal density using Tonelli and a generating rectangle class, and apply linear change of variables with the determinant computed spectrally.

references.title: Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §2.3, Equation (2.43)

items.title: Lloyd iteration is objective-decreasing and terminates
items.statement: Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, and supply any initial centers in $(\mathbb R^p)^K$. The tie-sensitive Lloyd algorithm defined on this page terminates after finitely many iterations. At each fixed-center assignment, the K-means objective does not increase, and it strictly decreases if any label changes. At each center update, the objective does not increase, and it strictly decreases if a nonempty-cluster center changes. At termination each label is a nearest-center label under the stated retention rule, and every nonempty-cluster center is its sample mean; no global-minimum conclusion is made.
items.strategy: For each fixed-center assignment use the nearest-center rule and strict tie retention; for each nonempty cluster use the finite least-squares normal equations. The finite label set and unique means rule out nonterminal recurrence.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

items.title: Exact EM updates for a finite Gaussian mixture
items.statement:
**Inputs.** Assume AC. Supply positive integers $n,p,K$, observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ whose affine span is $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ has $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), an initial finite Gaussian mixture parameter $\theta_0=((\pi_k^{(0)},\mu_k^{(0)},\Sigma_k^{(0)}))_{k=1}^K$ in the domain of the finite-mixture definition, and a positive integer $T$.

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,\ldots,T-1$, compute the responsibilities

$$\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}:=\frac{\pi_k^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})},\qquad N_k^{(t)}:=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}.$$

Then make the exact updates

$$\pi_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{N_k^{(t)}}{n},\qquad \mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}x_i,$$

$$\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}.$$

**Output.** Return the finite parameter sequence $(\theta_0,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_T)$. Every E-step uses the current parameter and every M-step uses that E-step's responsibilities. The affine-span hypothesis is imposed for the unrestricted positive-definite covariance update; constrained covariance domains require their own M-step. This definition makes no claim about convergence of parameters or a global maximum.
items.strategy: Procedure: at each finite step compute responsibilities at the current positive-weight/SPD mixture, then set weights to effective-count proportions and means/covariances to responsibility-weighted sample moments.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

items.title: The full-affine-span Gaussian-mixture M-step maximizes Q
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ have affine span $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ makes $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), and let $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$ be a finite Gaussian-mixture parameter with every $\pi_k>0$ and every $\Sigma_k$ symmetric positive definite. Define

$$\gamma_{ik}=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)},\qquad N_k=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik},\qquad \bar x_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}x_i,$$

and

$$S_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\bar x_k)(x_i-\bar x_k)^{\mathsf T}.$$

For a candidate parameter $\vartheta=((\rho_k,m_k,V_k))_{k=1}^K$ in the same domain, let

$$Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K\gamma_{ik}\log\!\left(\rho_k\phi_p(x_i;m_k,V_k)\right).$$

Then every $N_k$ is positive, $\sum_kN_k=n$, every $S_k$ is positive definite, and the unique global maximizer of $Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)$ over all positive mixture weights summing to one, means in $\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariances is

$$\rho_k^*=N_k/n,\qquad m_k^*=\bar x_k,\qquad V_k^*=S_k.$$

In particular the exact updates in the finite Gaussian-mixture EM procedure are well-defined and attain this maximum.
items.strategy: Separate the complete-data Q function into simplex, weighted-mean, and covariance terms. Use finite categorical KL, weighted-centering, full affine span, and strict log-det concavity in precision coordinates to prove a unique attained maximizer.

references.title: Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §9.2.2
Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing, §8.5.2

items.title: Exact Gaussian-mixture EM does not decrease observed log likelihood
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ have affine span $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ makes $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), and start from a finite Gaussian-mixture parameter $\theta_0=((\pi_k^{(0)},\mu_k^{(0)},\Sigma_k^{(0)}))_{k=1}^K$ with positive weights summing to one and symmetric positive-definite covariances. For $t=0,\ldots,T-1$, where $T\ge1$, set

$$\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}:=\frac{\pi_k^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})},\qquad N_k^{(t)}:=\sum_i\gamma_{ik}^{(t)},$$

and update

$$\pi_k^{(t+1)}:=N_k^{(t)}/n,\qquad \mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}x_i}{N_k^{(t)}},\qquad \Sigma_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}}{N_k^{(t)}}.$$

For each $t$, define

$$\ell(\theta_t;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})\right).$$

Every update is well-defined, every $\theta_t$ remains in the stated mixture domain, and

$$\ell(\theta_{t+1};x_{1:n})\ge\ell(\theta_t;x_{1:n})\qquad(0\le t<T).$$

No strict increase, parameter convergence, or global maximum conclusion is asserted.
items.strategy: Construct the normalized finite-label complete-data density and compute its marginal/posterior. Verify support, finite directional KL, positive finite marginals, and absolute log-integrability; identify Q with the local M-step objective and apply the current published EM identity.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing, §8.5.2 and §14.3.7
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §§9.2.2 and 9.4

title: K-means, Gaussian mixtures, and soft assignments — Examples

items.title: Tie retention gives distinct Lloyd fixed points
items.statement: For the data $x_1=0,x_2=1,x_3=2,x_4=3$ in $\mathbb R$ and $K=2$, use nearest-center initialization with smallest-index initialization ties, retain the current label on later ties, replace each nonempty center by its assigned-data mean, and leave empty centers unchanged. For clusters $C_1,C_2$ and centers $c_1,c_2$, define the cost by $J=\sum_{k=1}^2\sum_{x_i\in C_k}(x_i-c_k)^2$. Initial centers $(0,11/10)$ yield the fixed clusters $\{0\}$ and $\{1,2,3\}$ with centers $(0,2)$ and cost $2$. Initial centers $(3,19/10)$ yield the fixed clusters $\{3\}$ and $\{0,1,2\}$ with centers $(3,1)$ and cost $2$. Initial centers $(1/2,5/2)$ yield the fixed clusters $\{0,1\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ with centers $(1/2,5/2)$ and cost $1$. In the first two runs, the boundary observation is tied between the two updated centers and stays in its current cluster by the retention rule; each output is a fixed point, while the third has lower cost.
items.strategy: Compute nearest-label assignments, mean updates, subsequent tie retentions, terminal states, and squared costs for all three specified starts; the TikZ figure is only a display of those computations.

references.title: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing, §14.3.5
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §9.1

items.title: A tied observation keeps fractional Gaussian responsibilities
items.statement: Take one observation $x=0\in\mathbb R$, two Gaussian components with means $\mu_1=-1$ and $\mu_2=1$, common variance $\sigma^2>0$, and mixture weights $\pi_1=1/3$ and $\pi_2=2/3$. Their component density is $\phi_1(x;\mu,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2))$, and the responsibility of component $k$ is $\gamma_k=\pi_k\phi_1(0;\mu_k,\sigma^2)/\sum_{j=1}^2\pi_j\phi_1(0;\mu_j,\sigma^2)$. The two squared distances from the observation to the component means are both $1$. For every $\sigma>0$, the responsibility vector is exactly $(1/3,2/3)$; therefore as $\sigma\downarrow0$ it remains fractional rather than converging to $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$.
items.strategy: Substitute the one-dimensional Gaussian formula; equal distances give identical positive component densities, which cancel in the responsibility ratio. The finite low-variance theorem confirms the weighted tied-center limit.

references.title: Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §9.3.2 and Exercise 9.11
Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing, Exercise 13.1

items.title: A two-point sample has unbounded Gaussian-mixture likelihood
items.statement: For the observations $x_1=0,x_2=1\in\mathbb R$, use two Gaussian components of weights $1/2,1/2$, both with mean $0$, with variances $\varepsilon^2$ and $1$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Write $\phi_1(x;0,s^2)=(2\pi s^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-x^2/(2s^2))$, $f_\varepsilon(x)=\tfrac12\phi_1(x;0,\varepsilon^2)+\tfrac12\phi_1(x;0,1)$, and $L_\varepsilon=f_\varepsilon(0)f_\varepsilon(1)$. Every parameter in this family has positive weights and positive-definite one-dimensional covariances. The likelihood $L_\varepsilon$ is unbounded above as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; hence its log likelihood is unbounded above as well.
items.strategy: Lower-bound the mixture density at the collapsing observation by the shrinking-variance component and at the other observation by the fixed component; multiply and send epsilon to zero through positive values.

references.title: Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §9.2.2
Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., corrected 12th printing, §14.3.7
